0.title: That You May Know: The Epistle of Assurance
0.overview:
There is a letter in the New Testament that reads like the heartbeat of an old man who has seen everything and lost nothing. John — the apostle whom Jesus loved, the one who leaned against the Lord at the Last Supper, the one who stood at the foot of the cross when the others had fled — writes at the end of a long life with the urgency of a man who knows that what he carries is the most important thing in the world. He has handled the Word of Life with his own hands. He has seen the glory. And he cannot be silent.

The First Epistle of John was written to a community under assault — not from Rome, but from within. Teachers had arisen who denied the full humanity of Christ, claiming that the eternal Son had not truly come in the flesh, that the spiritual and the material could not really meet. They were sophisticated, confident, and wrong. When they left the fellowship, John writes to those who remain, not to condemn the departed but to assure the faithful: you are not the ones who have missed it. The letter is saturated with the word "know" — used over thirty times. John wants his readers to know that they have eternal life, that they are in fellowship with the Father and the Son, that the darkness is passing and the true light is already shining.

But assurance in John is never cheap. It is tested by three great evidences that run through the letter like interwoven cords: the moral test (do you walk in the light, keeping his commandments?), the social test (do you love your brothers and sisters?), and the doctrinal test (do you confess that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh?). These are not conditions for salvation but symptoms of it — the fingerprints of new birth on a redeemed life. The person who has truly been born of God will love, will obey, and will confess. Not perfectly — John is the one who tells us that if we say we have no sin we deceive ourselves — but genuinely and persistently.

At the theological centre of the letter stands the cross. "The blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin" (1:7). "He is the propitiation for our sins" (2:2). "He laid down his life for us" (3:16). "God sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins" (4:10). John circles back to the atoning death of Christ again and again, because the cross is the ground of everything — fellowship, forgiveness, assurance, love. The love of God is not an abstraction in 1 John; it is a specific act: the sending of the Son into the world to bear the wrath that our sins deserved so that we might live through him.

The theological lens throughout this commentary is Reformed and christological, drawing especially on John Stott's The Letters of John (Tyndale New Testament Commentaries), D.A. Carson, Sinclair Ferguson, and the preaching of Alistair Begg. The governing conviction is that 1 John was written to produce settled, humble, joyful assurance in the hearts of those who have truly come to Christ — and that such assurance, far from producing complacency, is the very fire that fuels a life of love.

1.title: The Word of Life and the God of Light
1.text: <sup>1</sup>That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands, concerning the word of life — <sup>2</sup>the life was made manifest, and we have seen it, and testify to it and proclaim to you the eternal life, which was with the Father and was made manifest to us — <sup>3</sup>that which we have seen and heard we proclaim also to you, so that you too may have fellowship with us; and indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ. <sup>4</sup>And we are writing these things so that our joy may be complete. <sup>5</sup>This is the message we have heard from him and proclaim to you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all. <sup>7</sup>But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin. <sup>8</sup>If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. <sup>9</sup>If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. <sup>10</sup>If we say we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us.
1.overview:
The letter opens not with a greeting but with a declaration — the breathless, stacked-up proclamation of a man who cannot contain what he has witnessed. Four times John insists on the physicality of his testimony: heard, seen, looked upon, touched. This is no vision, no spiritual impression, no mystical encounter. The eternal Word who was with the Father before all worlds became touchable. John's hands rested on him. The Gnostic teachers who had just left the community claimed special spiritual knowledge that transcended the material. John's answer is the incarnation: the eternal life appeared, and we handled it with these hands.

From this foundation John moves to the purpose of his proclamation: fellowship — with the Father, with the Son, and with one another. And then, immediately, the first great test. The God with whom we claim fellowship is light — pure, uncompromising, all-revealing light. In him is no darkness at all. Any claim to fellowship with this God that allows a comfortable cohabitation with sin is self-deception. But the answer to sin is not despair — it is the blood of Jesus his Son, which cleanses continually (present tense) from all sin, and the promise of forgiveness to all who confess.

verseByVerse.quote: That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands, concerning the word of life—the life was made manifest, and we have seen it, and testify to it and proclaim to you the eternal life, which was with the Father and was made manifest to us.
verseByVerse.commentary: John opens with a torrent of sense verbs — heard, seen, looked upon, touched — because the heresy he is combating denied exactly this: that the eternal Son truly entered material reality. The repetition is deliberate; it is the insistence of an eyewitness who will not let the incarnation be spiritualised away. Apo archēs — from the beginning — echoes the opening of the Gospel (“In the beginning was the Word”), identifying the one who became touchable with the eternal Word. The life was with the Father and was made manifest: the divine life broke into history, into human hands, into human ears. Stott observes that the accumulation of sensory language is John's proof that Christianity is not a philosophy or a spiritual mood but a set of historical facts about a real person.

verseByVerse.quote: That which we have seen and heard we proclaim also to you, so that you too may have fellowship with us; and indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary: The purpose of apostolic proclamation is not primarily intellectual persuasion but relational inclusion: so that you too may have fellowship with us. And this fellowship is not merely horizontal (with other believers) but vertical — with the Father and with his Son. To be in the church is to be in communion with God himself. The staggering claim here is that the same fellowship John has with the Father through the Son is the fellowship on offer to every reader. Keller notes that the gospel creates the deepest possible community, because it is not membership in an organisation but participation in a divine relationship that was eternal before the world began.

verseByVerse.quote: And we are writing these things so that our joy may be complete.
verseByVerse.commentary: John names joy as the goal of the letter. Not information, not correction alone, not institutional preservation — joy. And specifically our joy: the writer's joy is not complete until the readers are fully in the fellowship described in v. 3. This mirrors the High Priestly Prayer (“that my joy may be in them and their joy may be full,” Jn 17:13). Ferguson points out that this joy is not an emotion manufactured by the will but a consequence of being properly related to the Father through the Son; it is the overflow of right theology lived in real community.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the message we have heard from him and proclaim to you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.
verseByVerse.commentary: “God is light” — the most compressed theological statement in the epistle and the premise of everything that follows. Light in the Old Testament is associated with God's holiness, truth, and life-giving presence (Ps 27:1; 36:9). To say God is light is to say he is absolutely pure, perfectly transparent, entirely without moral shadow. The emphatic double negation — no darkness at all — rules out any zone of divine compromise. Sproul observes that this is not a poetic metaphor but a doctrinal claim: the character of God is the standard by which the character of the Christian life must be measured, which is why the tests of ch. 1–2 carry such moral weight.

verseByVerse.quote: If we say we have fellowship with him while we walk in darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary: The first of John's three “if we say” tests (vv. 6, 8, 10), each exposing a false claim. Claiming fellowship with the God who is light while walking in darkness is not merely inconsistency — it is a lie. The word walk (“peripatein”) is John's characteristic word for the pattern and direction of a life. A life oriented toward darkness cannot coexist with fellowship with the one in whom there is no darkness. Calvin: the test of our profession is always found in the habitual direction of the life, not in our verbal claims about our spiritual state.

verseByVerse.quote: But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin.
verseByVerse.commentary: The positive counterpart to v. 6. Walking in the light does not mean sinless perfection; it means living openly before God, with nothing hidden and no pretence. The remarkable consequence is twofold: fellowship with one another, and cleansing by Christ's blood. The two are inseparable — genuine community and ongoing forgiveness are both products of honest, light-oriented living. Notice that even those walking in the light need ongoing cleansing: “cleanses” is present tense, continuous. The blood of Jesus is not a one-time transaction but a permanent provision for the believer who remains in the light.

verseByVerse.quote: If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
verseByVerse.commentary: The second false claim is not the claim of non-Christians but of believers: “we have no sin.” The Gnostic opponents were likely claiming that their spiritual enlightenment placed them beyond the reach of sin. John's answer is blunt: such a claim is self-deception. The word planōmen — we deceive, we lead ourselves astray — implies that this is not innocent error but an active self-misleading. And its symptom is that “the truth is not in us” — the truth of God's word, which diagnoses every human being as a sinner (Ps 143:2; Rom 3:23), has not taken root in such a person.

verseByVerse.quote: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary: The most gracious verse in the chapter. Against the backdrop of self-deception (v. 8), John sets the promise of confession: God is faithful and just to forgive. Not merely willing — bound by his own character and covenant. Faithful: he promised forgiveness through Christ and will not revoke it. Just: because the penalty for sin has been fully paid at the cross, forgiving the confessor is not a waiving of justice but its satisfaction. Stott: “It is not mercy but justice which God exercises in the forgiveness of our sins, because the death of Christ has made it possible for God to be both just and the justifier.” The cleansing promised covers not just specific sins confessed but all unrighteousness — the deeper contamination beneath the surface acts.

verseByVerse.quote: If we say we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us.
verseByVerse.commentary: The third false claim escalates: not “we have no sin” (present state, v. 8) but “we have not sinned” (past action, the whole of life). To deny any personal history of sin is to contradict God's own testimony about the human condition (Rom 3:23; Ps 14:3). And contradicting God is not merely error — it is making him a liar. The phrase “his word is not in us” echoes v. 8 and ties back to v. 5: the message John is proclaiming has not been received. A person whose life leaves no room for the grace of v. 9 has not yet heard the gospel.

1.theology:
The Incarnation as Foundation. Everything in 1 John rests on the physical, historical, tangible reality of the incarnation. John's stacked verbs in verses 1–2 — heard, seen, looked upon, touched — are a theological rampart against every form of docetism (the heresy that Christ only appeared to be human). If Christ did not truly come in flesh, the blood shed on Calvary has no atoning value, the resurrection is a spirit's trick, and there is no real fellowship between God and humanity. The incarnation is not incidental to Christianity; it is its structural foundation. God became graspable so that we could grasp him — and through him, life.

The God Who is Light. John's declaration that "God is light, and in him is no darkness at all" has massive ethical implications. Fellowship with a God of absolute moral purity cannot coexist with a comfortable relationship with sin. The light of God is not a comfortable mood but a searching, penetrating, all-revealing reality. It is also a liberating one: in the light, where our sin is exposed, the blood of Jesus cleanses. Reformed theology has always insisted on the holiness of God as the backdrop against which the grace of God becomes luminous. You cannot appreciate the gospel without first standing in the light of who God is.
1.examples:
Then: The community John writes to had just experienced a painful split. People they had worshipped with, broken bread with, called brothers and sisters, had walked out. The departure of the false teachers left wounds and questions. Were the ones who stayed the ones who had missed the deeper truth? John's answer in chapter 1 is the apostolic testimony: we were there. We heard him, saw him, touched him. This is not speculation; it is witness. The assurance of the community rests not on their spiritual experiences but on the testimony of those who were eyewitnesses of the Word of Life.

Now: We live in a culture that treats the interior life as the truest life — feelings, impressions, spiritual experiences. The incarnation is John's counter-word: Christianity is tethered to history, to flesh, to blood, to an empty tomb. Our fellowship with God is not a feeling; it is a fact grounded in the historical reality of the Son of God made flesh. And the practice of confession — agreeing with God about what we are — is the daily discipline that keeps that fellowship living and real. Every day we come back to the same place: not to earn forgiveness, but to receive what has already been purchased.

2.title: Our Advocate, Our Obedience, Our Love
2.text: <sup>1</sup>My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. <sup>2</sup>He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world. <sup>3</sup>And by this we know that we have come to know him, if we keep his commandments. <sup>5</sup>But whoever keeps his word, in him truly the love of God is perfected. By this we may know that we are in him: <sup>6</sup>whoever says he abides in him ought to walk in the same way in which he walked. <sup>15</sup>Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. <sup>16</sup>For all that is in the world — the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life — is not from the Father but is from the world. <sup>17</sup>And the world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever. <sup>24</sup>Let what you heard from the beginning abide in you. If what you heard from the beginning abides in you, then you too will abide in the Son and in the Father. <sup>25</sup>And this is the promise that he made to us — eternal life.
2.overview:
Chapter 2 moves in three great movements. First, the pastoral heart of John: he wants his readers not to sin, but he is realistic enough to know they will, and he points them to the one who stands as their advocate before the Father — Jesus Christ the righteous, the propitiation for their sins. This is the most concentrated statement of substitutionary atonement in the Johannine letters, and it is placed here, at the beginning, as the ground of all that follows.

Second, John introduces the first of his three great tests of authentic Christianity: the test of obedience. Not sinless perfection, but a life characterized by the keeping of his commandments. The person who says "I know him" but does not keep his word is a liar. Third, John warns against the love of the world — a love that competes with and displaces the love of the Father. The world and all its desires are passing away; the one who does the will of God abides forever. The chapter ends with an appeal to hold fast to what was heard from the beginning: the apostolic gospel, not the novel teaching of the antichrists who have gone out.

verseByVerse.quote: My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world.
verseByVerse.commentary: John's double pastoral aim is captured in a single sentence: he writes so that they will not sin, but he immediately provides for when they do. The two truths must be held together — any account of the Christian life that removes either the call to holiness or the provision for failure is incomplete. The paraklētos — advocate, one who stands alongside — is Jesus Christ the righteous, pleading before the Father on the basis of his own righteousness, not the penitent's. Hilasmos (propitiation) means the satisfaction of God's just wrath against sin; the cross did not merely cover sin but absorbed its penalty. The scope — not for ours only but for the whole world — proclaims the sufficiency of the atonement for all who will believe.

verseByVerse.quote: And by this we know that we have come to know him, if we keep his commandments.
verseByVerse.commentary: John's first explicit test of assurance: the evidence of genuine knowledge of God is obedience to his commandments. This is not works-salvation — the keeping of commandments does not earn fellowship with God but evidences it. The Greek egnōkamen (we have come to know) is perfect tense, indicating a knowledge acquired and still possessed. Keller: the test is not whether we ever fail (we do), but whether obedience is the settled pattern and desire of the life — the direction of travel, not the perfection of arrival.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever says 'I know him' but does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him, but whoever keeps his word, in him truly the love of God is perfected.
verseByVerse.commentary: The two sides of v. 3 expanded into sharp contrasts. The person who claims to know God while living in habitual disobedience is simply lying — the claim and the life are irreconcilable. John has no interest in diplomatic softening here. But the positive is equally sharp: where the word of God is kept, the love of God is “perfected” — brought to its intended completion, its telos. God's love does not merely declare us righteous; it works in us until it reaches full expression in a life conformed to his word. Stott notes that “the love of God” here is most likely God's love for us, now perfected in us as it produces its fruit.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever says he abides in him ought to walk in the same way in which he walked.
verseByVerse.commentary: The claim to “abide in him” carries an ethical obligation: the pattern of Christ's own walk becomes the measure of the believer's walk. The aorist ekeinos periepatēsen (he walked) looks back to the historical life of Jesus — not a mystical ideal but the concrete obedience of the incarnate Son. This is John's Christological ethic: the imitation of Christ is not self-improvement by willpower but the natural consequence of union with him. Where genuine abiding exists, Christlike walking follows as the fruit follows the vine.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, I am writing you no new commandment, but an old commandment that you had from the beginning. The old commandment is the word that you have heard.
verseByVerse.commentary: The commandment John is about to describe (love one another) is old — not recently invented but there from the beginning: rooted in Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18, the two great love-commandments of Torah. John's point is that he is not innovating; he is calling them back to what they already received. The repetition of “from the beginning” in this chapter is significant: the opponents claimed to have new and superior knowledge, while John keeps pointing to the original, apostolic word received at conversion.

verseByVerse.quote: At the same time, it is a new commandment that I am writing to you, which is true in him and in you, because the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining.
verseByVerse.commentary: Yet the love commandment is also genuinely new — not chronologically new, but new in the sense that it has been filled with new content and new power by the coming of Christ. In him, love was embodied and demonstrated at its fullest (Jn 13:34, “love one another as I have loved you”). The eschatological frame matters: the darkness is passing away (present tense, already in motion) and the true light is already shining. The new age has dawned in Christ; the old age of darkness is being displaced. The commandment to love is a participation in this new world that is already, in Christ, a reality.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever says he is in the light and hates his brother is still in darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary: The claim to be in the light is tested by the most concrete of measures: the treatment of a fellow believer. Hatred of a brother while claiming spiritual illumination is not merely inconsistency — it is evidence that the claimed light has never arrived. The word misōn (hating) is present participle: a settled, habitual hatred, not a passing offence. John does not allow any divorce between vertical spirituality and horizontal relationships; the two form one seamless garment, and tearing the horizontal reveals that the vertical was never real.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever loves his brother abides in the light, and in him there is no cause for stumbling.
verseByVerse.commentary: The positive of v. 9. Loving the brother is the evidence of abiding in the light, and it carries a remarkable personal benefit: in the one who loves there is no skandalon — no stumbling-block, no cause for tripping. The darkness of hatred makes people stumble (v. 11) because they cannot see where they are going. Love, by contrast, keeps the moral vision clear. Stott observes that love and light are mutually reinforcing: the one who truly sees God (lives in his light) will love what God loves, and that love itself keeps the moral sight from clouding.

verseByVerse.quote: But whoever hates his brother is in the darkness and walks in the darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary: John returns to the negative with increasing intensity. The hater is not merely in the dark; he walks in it — the pattern of life is darkness. And the result is a kind of moral blindness: he does not know where he is going. Sin, particularly the sin of hatred and contempt, distorts moral perception; the longer one walks in it, the less one can see what is true. This is the opposite of the progressive clarity that love produces (v. 10). The darkness has blinded the eyes — past tense, a completed action with ongoing effects. Hatred, nursed long enough, destroys the capacity for spiritual sight.

verseByVerse.quote: I am writing to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven for his name's sake.
verseByVerse.commentary: John addresses the whole community as “little children” (teknia) — his affectionate term for the entire congregation, not just one age group. The first thing he says to them is not a command or a test but a declaration of grace: your sins are forgiven. The ground of forgiveness is not their merit or their longevity in faith but his name's sake — for the sake of Jesus Christ, whose name (character, authority, atoning work) is the sole basis of every pardon. Calvin: the assurance of forgiveness is the foundation on which all ethical exhortation must rest; commands addressed to the unforgiven only produce despair.

verseByVerse.quote: I am writing to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I am writing to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one.
verseByVerse.commentary: John addresses two stages of spiritual maturity. The “fathers” — those long in the faith — are characterised by depth of knowledge: they know him who is from the beginning, the eternal Christ. Mature faith is Christocentric and deep-rooted; it has had time to know not just about Christ but to know him. The “young men” are characterised by vigour: they have overcome the evil one. Active faith engages the spiritual battle and prevails. Ferguson notes that John is not flattering either group but describing what grace produces at each stage: depth in the long-seasoned, strength in the newly-fierce.

verseByVerse.quote: I write to you, children, because you know the Father. I write to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I write to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome the evil one.
verseByVerse.commentary: John repeats the three-fold address in a second pass (“I write,” past tense vs. “I am writing,” present). The children now are those who know the Father — the most basic of all Christian knowledge, the Abba-relationship granted in adoption (4:14; Rom 8:15). The young men receive the fuller description: they are strong; the word of God abides in them; they have overcome. The word of God abiding is the source of the strength and the means of the victory — Scripture is not merely information but a living power that equips the believer for the fight against the evil one (cf. Eph 6:17).

verseByVerse.quote: Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.
verseByVerse.commentary: “The world” here is not the created order (which God loves, Jn 3:16) but the age organised in rebellion against God — the system of values, desires, and allegiances that runs counter to the kingdom. The command is absolute: do not love it. And the reason is as stark as anything in the epistle: love of the world and love of the Father are mutually exclusive. Where the world-system holds the heart's primary allegiance, the Father's love has no room. Keller: this is not a call to cultural withdrawal but to a radical reordering of ultimate loyalty — everything in the world may be enjoyed, but nothing in it may be enthroned.

verseByVerse.quote: For all that is in the world—the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life—is not from the Father but is from the world.
verseByVerse.commentary: John anatomises worldliness into three streams: the desires of the flesh (appetite-driven craving, wanting what the body demands), the desires of the eyes (covetous longing, wanting what is seen), and the pride of life (alazoneia — the boasting arrogance of self-sufficiency, wanting to be seen). These three are not from the Father — they are not the desires he planted in us at creation but the distortions that sin introduced. Commentators from Augustine onward have noted the parallel with the temptation of Eve (Gen 3:6: “good for food... pleasing to the eyes... desirable to make one wise”) and the temptation of Christ (Matt 4). The pattern of worldliness is old; the remedy is the same counter-formation that overcame it in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: And the world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever.
verseByVerse.commentary: The decisive eschatological argument against worldliness: the world is passing away. Present tense — the process is already underway. To love what is dissolving is to invest in a depreciating asset. The contrast is stark: those who do God's will — whose life is oriented not toward the age that is ending but toward the age that is beginning — abide forever. The word menei (abides) echoes the “abide in him” of vv. 6, 10, 27, 28; to be rightly related to God is to participate in the only permanence there is. Sproul: “The universe is growing old; the believer who does God's will is growing young.”

verseByVerse.quote: Children, it is the last hour, and as you have heard that antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have come. From this we know that it is the last hour.
verseByVerse.commentary: John names the theological moment: the last hour. The singular article (“the last hour”) is eschatological — the final era inaugurated by Christ's first coming and closing with his return. The expected singular antichrist has been preceded by many antichrists, whose very appearance confirms the lateness of the hour. These antichrists are not pagan outsiders but former members of the community (v. 19), making their theological deviation all the more serious. The repetition — “it is the last hour” both at the start and end of the verse — is rhetorical urgency: the time for comfortable compromise has run out.

verseByVerse.quote: They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us. But they went out, that it might become plain that they all are not of us.
verseByVerse.commentary: John's interpretation of apostasy is theologically penetrating: their departure was not caused by external pressure but revealed an internal reality. They were never truly of the community, and their leaving made this plain. This is not an excuse for carelessness about retention, but it is a warning against reading perseverance as the mere product of social factors. Genuine belonging produces genuine perseverance; those who fall away finally reveal that they lacked the life they appeared to have. The providence of their departure is declared: “that it might become plain.” Even apostasy serves the purposes of God in clarifying the true from the false.

verseByVerse.quote: But you have been anointed by the Holy One, and you all have knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary: The contrast with the departed (v. 19) is sharp: but you. What the false teachers claimed — superior spiritual knowledge — is actually the possession of every believer through the Spirit's anointing. The “anointing” (chrisma) is the gift of the Holy Spirit who illumines the believer to receive and hold apostolic truth. John's point is quietly devastating to spiritual elitism: the knowledge that matters is not the property of a few enlightened ones but of all who have received the Spirit. “You all have knowledge” — every member of the community, not just its teachers.

verseByVerse.quote: I write to you, not because you do not know the truth, but because you know it, and because no lie is of the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary: John is not correcting ignorance; he is reinforcing what his readers already know. The letter is a reminder, not a revelation. This grounds his confidence in their ability to discern: they know the truth, and they know that lies cannot coexist with truth. “No lie is of the truth” is a logical axiom with theological weight: the false teaching being circulated is not a variation of the gospel or a supplementation of it; it is simply incompatible with it. Truth and falsehood are not points on a spectrum; they are binary opposites, and the readers' knowledge of the truth equips them to recognise the lie.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is the liar but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the antichrist, he who denies the Father and the Son.
verseByVerse.commentary: John identifies the definitive lie: the denial that Jesus is the Christ. The Christological confession is not one doctrine among many — it is the hinge of everything. Those who denied the full identity of Jesus (likely separating the human Jesus from the divine Christ, as later Docetists and Gnostics would) were denying the very mechanism of salvation. And to deny the Son is to forfeit the Father: the two cannot be separated. There is no other path to the Father than through the Son (Jn 14:6); denying the Son severs the only connection to the Father. Sproul: “The deity of Christ is not a doctrinal luxury; it is the load-bearing wall of the gospel.”

verseByVerse.quote: No one who denies the Son has the Father. Whoever confesses the Son has the Father also.
verseByVerse.commentary: The positive and negative stated with equal clarity. The Father and the Son are inseparable in the economy of salvation: access to the one is access to the other; rejection of the one is rejection of the other. This is not theological symmetry for its own sake but a statement about the structure of reality. The Son is not a pointer to the Father or a useful mediating concept; he is the only way the Father is known, loved, and reached. Confession of the Son is therefore the indispensable act of true religion — not a supplementary option for those who prefer a more Christocentric spirituality.

verseByVerse.quote: Let what you heard from the beginning abide in you. If what you heard from the beginning abides in you, then you too will abide in the Son and in the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary: The antidote to false teaching is not clever counter-argument but the tenacious retention of the original apostolic word. “From the beginning” appears again — John's refrain in this chapter. The original message received at conversion is the Spirit-given truth; the new teaching circulating is the deviation. The conditional is a promise: if the original message abides, you will abide — in the Son and in the Father. Holding fast to right doctrine is the means of holding fast to the persons of the Trinity. Doctrine and devotion cannot ultimately be separated.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the promise that he made to us—eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary: The content of the promise that the apostolic message carries: eternal life. Not eternal existence (which the wicked also have, in a sense), but eternal life — the life of the age to come, the life that is God's own life shared with his people, which has already begun in those who believe (Jn 5:24, “has passed from death to life”). This promise is the opposite of what the false teachers offer: their innovation cannot deliver what only the Son, rightly confessed, provides. The promise is secured not by the believer's faithfulness in holding to it but by the faithfulness of the one who made it.

verseByVerse.quote: I write these things to you about those who are trying to deceive you.
verseByVerse.commentary: John names his purpose plainly: the false teachers are trying to deceive. The word planōntōn (those leading astray) uses the same root as the “we deceive ourselves” of 1:8 — the same deception, but now actively attempted by others. John does not soften this: those who deny the Son and offer an alternative spiritual path are not sincere but mistaken seekers — they are deceivers. Naming the threat clearly is an act of pastoral love; it equips the community to resist rather than absorb the false teaching out of misplaced charity.

verseByVerse.quote: But the anointing that you received from him abides in you, and you have no need that anyone should teach you. But as his anointing teaches you about everything, and is true, and is no lie—just as it has taught you, abide in him.
verseByVerse.commentary: John does not mean that the community needs no teachers at all (cf. 1 Cor 12:28; Eph 4:11) but that they have no need of the false teachers and their supplementary “deeper knowledge.” The Spirit's anointing — the internal illumination given to every believer — teaches about everything that pertains to salvation and godliness. The Spirit does not bring new revelation but confirms and illumines the apostolic word already received. The chapter ends where it begins: “abide in him” — the remedy for false teaching is not intellectual victory but sustained, Spirit-kept union with the Son.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, little children, abide in him, so that when he appears we may have confidence and not shrink from him in shame at his coming.
verseByVerse.commentary: The eschatological horizon sets the stakes for abiding. The return of Christ is not a distant abstraction but the event toward which all of John's exhortation points. At that appearing, there will be parrēsia (confidence, bold openness) or shrinking in shame — and which it will be depends on whether one has abided in him between now and then. This is not works-righteousness: the confidence is not earned by moral performance but by genuine union with Christ maintained through the ongoing reception of his word and the Spirit's work. The shame is not punishment but the inevitable awkwardness of meeting the one whose commands you have spent your life ignoring.

verseByVerse.quote: If you know that he is righteous, you may be sure that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of him.
verseByVerse.commentary: A key principle of John's ethical logic: the character of the Father is reproduced in the children. If God is righteous — and he is — then those born of him will practice righteousness. The new birth is not a change of status only but a change of nature; the divine life implanted in the believer tends inevitably toward the character of the one who gave it. This is John's first mention of the new birth in the epistle, and it grounds ethics in ontology: we live rightly not merely because we are told to but because we have been made, in a deep sense, righteous — partakers of the divine nature (2 Pet 1:4).

2.theology:
Advocacy and Propitiation. The paired terms of 2:1–2 give us the two aspects of Christ's saving work seen from different angles. As advocate, he represents us before the Father — our case is in his hands, and he is qualified to plead it because he is righteous. As propitiation, he has already dealt with the ground of the accusation — the wrath of God against our sin has been absorbed at the cross. These are not two separate acts but two perspectives on the one act of the cross. The same sacrifice that satisfied divine justice now grounds our ongoing access to divine mercy. Reformed theology has always insisted that the atonement is both objective (propitiation — something accomplished outside us, in history, on a cross) and applied (advocacy — an ongoing ministry of Christ on our behalf). Both are necessary; together they produce the settled assurance John wants his readers to have.

The Three Tests. John's three tests — obedience (2:3–6), love (2:9–11), and belief (2:22–23) — are not a checklist for earning assurance but symptoms of new birth. Just as a doctor looks for signs of life, John looks for the signs that genuine regeneration has occurred. These tests are not meant to produce anxiety but clarity: not "have I been good enough?" but "is there genuine fruit of the Spirit in my life?" The tests are cumulative and mutually reinforcing — genuine obedience produces love; genuine love flows from right belief; genuine belief manifests in how we treat the brothers and sisters.
2.examples:
Then: The antichrists who had left the community had claimed a superior knowledge of God. Their departure seemed, to some, like the enlightened ones leaving the unenlightened behind. John's response is pastoral and pointed: the ones who left proved by their leaving that they were never truly of the community (2:19). This is not cruelty but theology — genuine new birth produces perseverance. The ones who remained, confused and perhaps diminished, were the ones who had "the anointing from the Holy One" and knew the truth (2:20). The test of authenticity is not sophistication but faithfulness to the beginning.

Now: We live in a world of novelty — new spiritualities, new therapies, new paths to self-actualization. The church is perpetually tempted to trade the apostolic gospel for something more culturally current, more psychologically satisfying, more intellectually respectable. John's word is the same: let what you heard from the beginning abide in you. The gospel does not need to be updated; it needs to be inhabited. The depth we seek is not found by moving beyond the cross — it is found by going deeper into it.

3.title: Children of God, Love in Deed
3.text: <sup>1</sup>See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are. The reason why the world does not know us is that it did not know him. <sup>2</sup>Beloved, we are God's children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. <sup>3</sup>And everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure. <sup>14</sup>We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers. <sup>16</sup>By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers. <sup>17</sup>But if anyone has the world's goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God's love abide in him? <sup>18</sup>Little children, let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth.
3.overview:
Chapter 3 opens with one of the most arresting exclamations in all of Scripture: See what kind of love — the Greek word suggests something foreign, exotic, surprising, from another world entirely. The love that makes sinful creatures children of the holy God is not an extension of ordinary human affection. It is a different category of love altogether, an invasion from another realm. And it is not merely a legal status: "we are" — present tense, already, actually, really. The children of God are hidden to the world because the world did not recognize the Son of God either. The family resemblance is not yet complete — what we will be has not appeared — but the hope of Christlikeness at the appearing shapes the life of the believer now.

The chapter then descends from the heights of adoption to the concrete test of love: do we lay down our lives for the brothers? John defines love not by a feeling but by the cross — "he laid down his life for us" — and then applies the definition with bracing directness: if you have material resources and see a brother in need and close your heart, how does the love of God abide in you? Love in deed and truth, not in word and talk. The cross makes love costly, and costly love is the mark of those who have truly understood the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are. The reason why the world does not know us is that it did not know him.
verseByVerse.commentary: Idete — look, behold, consider carefully. John calls for active, attentive amazement at the love that has been lavished. The word potapēn (what kind of) is used of things foreign or extraordinary — a love of a category not native to this world. The content of that love is not a feeling but a status: we are called children of God, and so we are. The declaration is not merely legal but ontological; the adopted status is real. The world's failure to recognise believers is explained by its prior failure to recognise the Father: the family resemblance is there, but those who cannot see the Father cannot see his children.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, we are God's children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.
verseByVerse.commentary: The “now” and the “not yet” in perfect tension. We are children of God now — present tense, certain, real. But what the full expression of that sonship will look like has not yet been disclosed. The transformation at Christ's return will be comprehensive: we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. The beatific vision and the final conformity to Christ are inseparable; seeing the glorified Christ in his fullness will itself accomplish the final sanctification. Sproul: “The vision of God is not the reward for becoming like him; it is the means by which we are made like him.”

verseByVerse.quote: And everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure.
verseByVerse.commentary: Eschatological hope has present moral effect. The one who genuinely hopes for the appearing of Christ (v. 2) purifies himself now — the hope is not passive waiting but active moral orientation. The standard is arresting: as he is pure. Not “as pure as possible for a human being,” but with Christ's own purity as the target. This is not perfectionism in the sense of achieved sinlessness (ch. 1 ruled that out) but perfectionism in the sense of direction: the genuine hope of seeing Christ trains the moral vision on his character as the standard toward which the life is being shaped.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who makes a practice of sinning also practices lawlessness; sin is lawlessness.
verseByVerse.commentary: John defines sin theologically: anomia — lawlessness, the refusal of God's authority. Sin is not primarily a social infraction or a psychological malfunction; it is the rejection of divine lordship. The equation is important: sin is not merely the violation of specific rules but the spirit of self-governance that places the self above God's claim. “Makes a practice of sinning” translates a present participle (“the one sinning”) — indicating the characteristic pattern of a life, not an isolated act. The person whose life is fundamentally oriented toward self-rule is living in fundamental opposition to God.

verseByVerse.quote: You know that he appeared to take away sins, and in him there is no sin.
verseByVerse.commentary: The purpose of the incarnation stated with precision: he appeared hina (in order that) he might take away sins. The atonement is not an afterthought or a divine response to an unforeseen crisis but the purpose for which the Son came into the world. Arē (take away) implies removal, not merely coverage — the guilt lifted, the power broken, the record cleared. And the one who came to take away sin has no sin in himself — this is the prerequisite: only the sinless one can bear the sins of others without being contaminated by them. The impeccability of Christ is not a theological curiosity but the very basis of the atonement's effectiveness.

verseByVerse.quote: No one who abides in him keeps on sinning; no one who keeps on sinning has either seen him or known him.
verseByVerse.commentary: John states the incompatibility between abiding in Christ and habitual sin with paradoxical directness. He is not teaching sinless perfectionism (1:8–10 rules that out absolutely); he is making a claim about the direction and pattern of the regenerate life. The person who truly abides in Christ — who lives in living, trusting union with the Son — cannot also live in the pattern of sin, because Christ and sin are incompatible. The negative is equally diagnostic: anyone whose life is characterised by ongoing, unrepentant sin shows thereby that they have not truly seen or known Christ. Seeing and knowing here (as elsewhere in John) are relational, not merely cognitive.

verseByVerse.quote: Little children, let no one deceive you. Whoever practices righteousness is righteous, as he is righteous.
verseByVerse.commentary: A warning against the deception that separates righteousness from the righteous — the false teaching that claimed a spiritual status disconnected from ethical life. John's answer is direct: the one who practices righteousness is righteous. The practice is the evidence of the status. And the standard is again Christ himself: righteous as he is righteous. This is not perfectionism but Christological conformity as the goal. Ferguson: “John is not saying we earn righteousness by practicing it; he is saying that real righteousness, given by God, always produces its own evidence in the pattern of life.”

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever makes a practice of sinning is of the devil, for the devil has been sinning from the beginning. The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil.
verseByVerse.commentary: The family origin of habitual sin: the devil, who has been sinning — present tense, continuous, unrepentant — from the beginning. The devil is sin's originator and its patron; those whose lives are characterised by sin bear his family resemblance (cf. Jn 8:44). But the great declaration of v. 8b counters this: the Son of God appeared precisely in order to destroy the works of the devil. Lysē — to loose, undo, dissolve. Every work the devil has built — sin, death, bondage, accusation — is under demolition. The incarnation is cosmic warfare, and its outcome is certain: the Son destroys what the devil has done.

verseByVerse.quote: No one born of God makes a practice of sinning, for God's seed abides in him; and he cannot keep on sinning, because he has been born of God.
verseByVerse.commentary: The positive ground for v. 6: the reason the regenerate person cannot keep on sinning is that “God's seed abides in him.” The image of seed (sperma) conveys both origin (born of God) and ongoing life-principle (abiding). The new birth is not a past transaction only but an ongoing reality — the divine life continues to work in the one it has entered. The “cannot keep on sinning” is not inability in an absolute sense (the regenerate person certainly can and does sin) but inability in the sense of incompatibility with the deepest nature the new birth has given: the life of God in the soul tends inexorably toward God, not away from him.

verseByVerse.quote: By this it is evident who are the children of God, and who are the children of the devil: whoever does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is the one who does not love his brother.
verseByVerse.commentary: The diagnostic is plain and public: the children of God and the children of the devil are distinguished by observable patterns — practicing righteousness and loving the brother. The two criteria are inseparable, as vv. 11–18 will develop. The starkness of the “children of the devil” language is not vindictive; it is the same realism that characterises the whole chapter: behind the ethical surface of every life is a spiritual paternity, and that paternity is disclosed by the direction of the life. John allows no middle ground, no third category of respectable but unregenerate humanity.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is the message that you have heard from the beginning, that we should love one another.
verseByVerse.commentary: “From the beginning” again — the love commandment is not a new development but the original message of the apostolic proclamation. John grounds the command to love one another not in natural human solidarity but in the gospel itself: this is what you heard when you first received Christ. Love is not an addendum to the Christian life but its core social expression. The fact that it was proclaimed “from the beginning” also serves as a warning: the false teachers, with their claim to advanced knowledge, have moved away from this foundational message. True spirituality always returns, not advances away from, the love command.

verseByVerse.quote: We should not be like Cain, who was of the evil one and murdered his brother. And why did he murder him? Because his own deeds were evil and his brother's righteous.
verseByVerse.commentary: Cain is the paradigm of the unregenerate response to the righteous. His murder was not the product of a sudden rage but the expression of a nature: “his own deeds were evil.” The righteousness of Abel did not produce admiration in Cain but hatred — the light of a righteous life is experienced as accusation by one committed to darkness. John identifies Cain as a child of the evil one (cf. Jn 8:44), the first fruit of the devil's family pattern. This is the deep root of the world's hatred of believers (v. 13): righteousness, simply by being what it is, provokes the animosity of those who have chosen its opposite.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be surprised, brothers, that the world hates you.
verseByVerse.commentary: The hatred of the world is not a sign of God's disfavour or of Christian failure; it is a structural consequence of being in the right family. Jesus promised it (“If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you,” Jn 15:18); John repeats it as pastoral instruction: do not be surprised. The surprise would be the real problem — it would mean the believer had forgotten whose child they are and whose enemy the world is. The appropriate response to the world's hatred is not surprise, not retaliation, not assimilation — but the kind of love that continues to pray for its enemies (Matt 5:44).

verseByVerse.quote: We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers. Whoever does not love abides in death.
verseByVerse.commentary: The proof of new life is love for fellow believers. Not a feeling of benevolence but the practical, self-giving love that the rest of the chapter will describe. The metaphysical transaction — from death to life — is verified by the ethical evidence: love. This is John's consistent method: invisible realities (the new birth, abiding in God, the love of the Father) are confirmed by visible evidence (righteousness, love, obedience). The negative is equally stark: the one who does not love abides in death — the present state, the ongoing condition, the spiritual address. Death and life are not merely future destinies but present realities in which one is currently located.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him.
verseByVerse.commentary: John echoes Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount (Matt 5:21–22): hatred in the heart constitutes murder at the level of will and desire. The logic is consistent with John's characteristic moral realism: the inner disposition matters as much as the outward act, because the disposition discloses the nature of the soul. And murder, John says straightforwardly, is incompatible with eternal life. This is not teaching that a believer who struggles with anger is condemned; it is teaching that a life characterised by settled contempt and hatred for a fellow human being — with no repentance and no movement toward love — reveals the absence of the life of God.

verseByVerse.quote: By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary: The definition of love is not found in abstract philosophy or even in human experience at its best; it is found in the cross. By this we know love: Christ's self-giving death is the epistemological event that teaches us what love actually is. And this definition carries an immediate moral implication: we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers. The same Greek word (tithēmi) used of Christ's laying down his life (Jn 10:11, 15, 17–18) is now applied to the believer. This is not mere sentiment; it is the logic of union with Christ, in whom we have received a love that must now flow through us to others.

verseByVerse.quote: But if anyone has the world's goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God's love abide in him?
verseByVerse.commentary: John brings the grand abstraction of v. 16 to its most concrete test: the brother in front of you, in material need, seen by you, and your response. Kleisēi ta splanchna — closes his bowels (the seat of compassion in the ancient world) — is a vivid image of the deliberate shutting-off of the instinct to help. John's rhetorical question expects the obvious answer: God's love cannot abide in someone who sees concrete need and deliberately ignores it. The love defined by the cross is not a feeling that remains private; it must move through the hands and the wallet.

verseByVerse.quote: Little children, let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth.
verseByVerse.commentary: The application of vv. 16–17 in one crisp command. Verbal love — expressing care, saying the right things, talking about community — is insufficient and potentially deceptive. Real love is in deed: it does something for the person in need. And in truth: it is genuine, not performed for approval. John includes himself (“let us”) — the apostle is not exempt from this standard. This verse is the practical core of the chapter's ethic: love is not a theological category but a pattern of action, and it is verified by what the hands do, not what the mouth says.

verseByVerse.quote: By this we shall know that we are of the truth and reassure our heart before him; for whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything.
verseByVerse.commentary: The “by this” refers back to the love in deed and truth of v. 18. When we love concretely and genuinely, we have ground to “reassure our heart before him” — to still the accusations of conscience in God's presence. The pastoral heart of v. 20 is extraordinary: John acknowledges that the believer's heart may condemn them (the conscience that says “you have not loved enough, done enough, been enough”). But God is greater than our heart — his knowledge of us is more comprehensive and more accurate than our self-assessment. He knows the love we have tried to show, the faith beneath the failures, the genuine orientation of the will. This is not a licence for cheap grace but a comfort for the tender conscience.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God.
verseByVerse.commentary: The positive corollary of v. 20: when conscience is at peace — not because of sinless perfection but because the life is genuinely oriented toward love and obedience — there is parrēsia (bold confidence) before God. This is the same word used in 2:28 for confidence at Christ's coming; here it describes the daily posture of prayer. The believer who is walking in the light (1:7), loving in deed (3:18), and keeping the commandments (3:22) may draw near to God without cowering. Conscience is not infallible (v. 20), but when it is at peace, it is a gift — and John does not want his readers to manufacture false guilt where none is warranted.

verseByVerse.quote: And whatever we ask we receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do what pleases him.
verseByVerse.commentary: Answered prayer is linked to obedience — not as a mechanical transaction (obey enough, receive the answer) but as a relational congruence: the one who keeps God's commandments is living in alignment with God's will, and therefore their requests are shaped by that will. This is not a formula for getting what we want through moral performance; it is a description of what prayer looks like from inside a life ordered around pleasing God. Such a person asks for what God would give, because their desires have been shaped by his word. Keller: “The purpose of prayer is not to get God to do our will; it is to bring our will into alignment with his, so that when we ask, we ask for what he was already glad to give.”

verseByVerse.quote: And this is his commandment, that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another, just as he has commanded us.
verseByVerse.commentary: The plural “commandments” of v. 22 is now resolved into its essential content: one commandment with two inseparable aspects — faith in Christ and love for one another. These are not two separate commandments ranked in order but two dimensions of one response to the gospel. Faith without love is theoretical; love without faith is rootless. Together they constitute the full shape of the Christian life: vertical trust in the Son, horizontal care for the brother. That this is called a single commandment (singular) suggests that in God's mind they are one response — genuine faith always produces love, and genuine love is always grounded in faith.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever keeps his commandments abides in God, and God in him. And by this we know that he abides in us, by the Spirit whom he has given us.
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter closes with the mutual indwelling: the obedient believer abides in God and God abides in the believer. This is the Johannine shorthand for the deepest possible relationship — not external association but interpenetration of life (cf. Jn 15:4–7). And the assurance of this abiding is not self-generated confidence but Spirit-confirmed: we know it by the Spirit whom he has given us. The Holy Spirit is the divine attestation of the divine relationship — the one who bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God (Rom 8:16), and who produces in us the love and obedience that confirm the abiding.

3.theology:
Adoption and Transformation. The doctrine of adoption — huiothesia — is one of the richest in the New Testament, and 3:1–3 is one of its highest expressions. To be called children of God is not a metaphor of religious devotion; it is a declaration of a new ontological status. We have been brought into the family of God — not as servants, not as subjects, but as children who share in the inheritance of the Son. And adoption in John is both present reality ("so we are," v.1) and future consummation ("what we will be has not yet appeared," v.2). The "not yet" of our glorification does not undermine the "already" of our adoption; the hope of the appearing purifies the life of the one who holds it.

Love Defined by the Cross. John's definition of love in verse 16 is one of the most consequential sentences in the New Testament. He does not say "God is love, therefore love is whatever feels loving." He says love is defined by a specific act: the laying down of the life of the Son. The cross is love's definition, love's measure, and love's demand. Reformed theology has always insisted that the love of God is not sentimentality but holy self-giving at infinite cost. Every theology of love that avoids the cross will eventually become a theology of tolerance — and tolerance is not love. Love is the cross, and the cross makes demands.
3.examples:
Then: The community John writes to had experienced the pain of betrayal — people they had loved had left. The temptation in such a situation is to turn inward, to protect the heart, to love in word only and keep the real self safely guarded. John's word to them is the cross: he laid down his life. Not as an inspiration to imitate from a safe distance, but as the very definition and pattern of what love is. The ones who remained in the fellowship were called to love one another with an openness that made them vulnerable — precisely because that is what love, defined by the cross, requires.

Now: We live in a therapeutic culture that defines love primarily as acceptance and validation. John defines it as sacrifice. The question is not "do I feel warmly toward my brother?" but "am I laying anything down for my brother?" The test of love is not interior but behavioural — not word and talk but deed and truth. A closed hand toward a brother in need, whatever feelings accompany it, is not love in John's sense. The cross makes love costly, specific, and concrete.

4.title: Testing the Spirits and the Love of God
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, for many false prophets have gone out into the world. <sup>2</sup>By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, <sup>7</sup>Beloved, let us love one another, for love is from God, and whoever loves has been born of God and knows God. <sup>8</sup>Anyone who does not love does not know God, because God is love. <sup>9</sup>In this the love of God was made manifest among us, that God sent his only Son into the world, so that we might live through him. <sup>10</sup>In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. <sup>18</sup>There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear. For fear has to do with punishment, and whoever fears has not been perfected in love. <sup>19</sup>We love because he first loved us.
4.overview:
Chapter 4 begins with a warning and ends with a declaration, and between them lies the most concentrated exposition of the love of God in the New Testament. The warning: test the spirits, for not every spirit that claims to be from God is from God. The test is doctrinal — does the spirit confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh? The incarnation is the fault line between truth and error, between the Spirit of God and the spirit of antichrist. Every age has its sophisticated spiritualities that try to have God without the incarnation, the cross without the propitiation, love without the costly sacrifice of the Son. John's answer is always the same: go back to the flesh, go back to the blood, go back to what was from the beginning.

Then, from verse 7, the chapter soars. Three times John says "God is love" (vv. 8, 16) — not "God is loving" but "God is love," love as the very essence of who he is. But he never lets this become abstraction. The love of God is immediately defined by its supreme expression: the sending of the Son to be the propitiation for our sins. And the love of God, so defined, demands a response — not fear, which has to do with punishment, but the freedom of those who know that the punishment has been absorbed, the debt paid, the wrath of God fully satisfied in the beloved Son.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, for many false prophets have gone out into the world.
verseByVerse.commentary: The command to test the spirits is both a warning about credulity and an affirmation that discernment is possible. “Do not believe every spirit” assumes that not every spirit claiming divine authority is telling the truth. The proliferation of false prophets is not an aberration of church history but a constant feature of it; Jesus predicted it (Matt 7:15), Paul warned against it (2 Cor 11:13–14), and John confirms it. The remedy is not scepticism of everything supernatural but careful testing — the community has the Spirit (3:24) and the apostolic teaching (2:20, 27) needed to distinguish true from false. Spiritual experience, however vivid, must be submitted to doctrinal testing.

verseByVerse.quote: By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist, which you heard was coming and now is in the world already.
verseByVerse.commentary: The test is christological: does the spirit confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh? The perfect tense (elēluthota) insists on the permanent reality of the incarnation — not that a spiritual being temporarily took on a fleshly appearance, but that the eternal Son permanently became human. The heresy being countered (likely proto-Docetism) denied the genuine humanity of Christ, seeing the material body as unworthy of the divine. John's test exposes this: a spirit that refuses the full incarnation is not from God but is the spirit of antichrist. The test is not about the subjective experience of the teaching but its Christological content.

verseByVerse.quote: Little children, you are from God and have overcome them, for he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.
verseByVerse.commentary: The pastoral encouragement after the warning: the readers have already overcome the false prophets. This is past tense — the victory is declared, not merely promised. The ground of the victory is not their own spiritual sophistication but the one who is in them: the Holy Spirit, greater than the spirit of antichrist that energises the false prophets. “Greater is he who is in you than he who is in the world” — this is not a comparative compliment but a statement about the absolute disparity between the Spirit of God and the spirit of the age. The indwelling Spirit is the believer's security against deception; he is not equally matched against the opposing spirit but infinitely superior.

verseByVerse.quote: They are from the world; therefore they speak from the world, and the world listens to them.
verseByVerse.commentary: The false prophets' origin (the world) explains their message (worldly) and their audience (the world listens). This is not snobbery or tribalism; it is a description of spiritual resonance: like recognises like. The world-system, organised in rebellion against God, responds warmly to teachers who reshape the gospel in terms it finds acceptable. The popularity of false teaching is therefore not evidence of its truth but of its alignment with the world. When the false prophets' message is well-received by those outside the community, it is a diagnostic sign, not an endorsement.

verseByVerse.quote: We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. By this we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of error.
verseByVerse.commentary: John speaks apostolically: the community's response to the apostolic message is a diagnostic tool for discernment. Those who know God recognise and receive the apostolic teaching; those who do not know God reject it. This is not sectarian arrogance but the application of spiritual resonance in the other direction: just as worldly people respond to worldly teaching, those who are truly of God respond to the God-given apostolic word. The criterion for distinguishing the Spirit of truth from the spirit of error is therefore partly exegetical (the content of the teaching, vv. 2–3) and partly ecclesiological (its reception by the community of the Spirit).

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, let us love one another, for love is from God, and whoever loves has been born of God and knows God.
verseByVerse.commentary: The great theme of the chapter — love — arrives after the doctrinal testing of vv. 1–6. Doctrine and love are not alternative emphases for different types of Christians; they belong together. The basis of the command to love is theological: love is from God. It originates in him; when we love, we are participating in something that comes from outside ourselves. And the evidence is again stated: whoever loves has been born of God and knows God. The new birth is the source of love, and love is the evidence of the new birth; love and knowing God are inseparable because God himself is love (v. 8).

verseByVerse.quote: Anyone who does not love does not know God, because God is love.
verseByVerse.commentary: “God is love” — the most concentrated theological statement in the epistle. Not merely that God is loving (an attribute among many) but that love is the deepest characterisation of his being. This is not a sentimental equation of God with a warm feeling; it is a statement about the eternal communion of the Trinity, in which love is the mode of relation between Father, Son, and Spirit from before the foundation of the world. The practical consequence is severe: anyone who does not love does not know God. The inability or refusal to love is a symptom of not having encountered the one whose very being is love. You cannot truly know love-itself and remain unmoved toward love.

verseByVerse.quote: In this the love of God was made manifest among us, that God sent his only Son into the world, so that we might live through him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The definition of divine love is not found by introspection or philosophy but in a historical event: God sent his only Son into the world. The word monogenē (only Son, only-begotten) marks the costliness of the gift — not one of many but the unique, irreplaceable Son. The purpose is life: so that we might live through him. The natural human condition without Christ is one of spiritual death (Eph 2:1); the sending of the Son is the provision of life to the dead. Love defined by the cross is not an emotion but a mission — the costly, purposeful, self-giving act of a God who sent what was most precious to rescue what was most lost.

verseByVerse.quote: In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.
verseByVerse.commentary: The direction of love is decisively established: it runs from God to us, not from us to God. This is the Copernican revolution of the gospel — we are not at the centre, reaching upward; God is at the centre, reaching down. The human contribution to salvation is not our prior love for God but our need for his love. And the mechanism of that love is propitiation — the sending of the Son to satisfy the just wrath of God against sin, so that sinners could be received into the family of God. Stott: “The cross is the supreme proof of the love of God, because it is the supreme demonstration of what love is willing to cost.”

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.
verseByVerse.commentary: The logic of grace driving the ethic of love. “If” is not conditional doubt but logical inference: since God so loved us. The love we have received from God creates both the obligation and the capacity to love others. The obligation: those who have been loved at infinite cost have no ground for withholding love from those who have cost them nothing. The capacity: the love of God, received through the Spirit (Rom 5:5), is the very resource that enables horizontal love. We do not generate love for one another from within ourselves; we pass on what we have first received.

verseByVerse.quote: No one has ever seen God; if we love one another, God abides in us and his love is perfected in us.
verseByVerse.commentary: The invisible God becomes visible through the community of love. This is John's most arresting claim about the church: when believers love one another, God himself is made present and perceptible in the world in a way that no individual spiritual experience or impressive programme can achieve. His love is “perfected” (teteleiōmenē) in us — brought to its intended completion, its goal. The love that originates in God (v. 7), was manifested in the Son (v. 9), and was received by us (v. 10) reaches its telos when it flows through us to one another. The church's love is not merely a moral imperative; it is the divine love completing its circuit.

verseByVerse.quote: By this we know that we abide in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary: The assurance of mutual indwelling is Spirit-based. We do not know we abide in God and he in us by introspection alone, or by moral achievement, but by the presence of the Holy Spirit whom he has given. The Spirit is the divine gift that both constitutes and confirms the relationship: he is the one who produces the love of v. 7, the confession of v. 2, and the witness of 3:24. The “by this we know” formula, recurring throughout the epistle, grounds assurance in objective, God-given realities rather than in the fluctuating feelings of the believer.

verseByVerse.quote: And we have seen and testify that the Father has sent his Son to be the Savior of the world.
verseByVerse.commentary: John returns to his eyewitness authority: we have seen and testify. The apostolic proclamation rests on historical observation, not spiritual intuition. The title “Savior of the world” is rare in John's writings (cf. Jn 4:42) and sweeps past all ethnic or national limitation: the Son's saving mission is not restricted to Israel or to any one people but encompasses the world. This universal scope does not imply universal salvation but universal sufficiency and universal offer: the Savior who came for the world is able to save anyone who comes to him in faith.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God.
verseByVerse.commentary: The christological confession of v. 2 is now connected explicitly to the mutual indwelling of vv. 12–13. To confess Jesus as Son of God is not merely to affirm a doctrinal proposition; it is the act by which one is drawn into the life of God. The confession is the public, verbal expression of the faith that unites the believer to the Son and, through the Son, to the Father. Abiding in God is the result of this confessing faith — not a higher state for the spiritually advanced but the basic reality of every true believer who opens their mouth and says, with full intent, “Jesus is the Son of God.”

verseByVerse.quote: So we have come to know and to believe the love that God has for us. God is love, and whoever abides in love abides in God, and God abides in him.
verseByVerse.commentary: “We have come to know and to believe” — two overlapping but distinct activities. Knowledge here is relational and experiential (egnōkamen); belief is committed trust (pepisteukamen). Together they describe the full response to the love of God: intellectual recognition and personal commitment. The statement “God is love” (repeated from v. 8) now frames the mutual indwelling: to abide in love is to abide in God, because God and love cannot be separated. This is not the same as saying that all love is of God in some generic sense; it is saying that the specific love defined by vv. 9–10 (sacrificial, propitious, from God toward sinners) is the environment in which genuine union with God occurs.

verseByVerse.quote: By this is love perfected with us, so that we may have confidence for the day of judgment, because as he is so also are we in this world.
verseByVerse.commentary: The perfection of love (its completion in us) has an eschatological purpose: parrēsia (bold confidence) at the day of judgment. The believer stands before the judgment seat not in their own righteousness but in the righteousness of the one with whom they are united: “as he is so also are we in this world.” Not as he was — as he is: the exalted, glorified, vindicated, righteous Son in whom the believer is hidden (Col 3:3). The confidence of the last day is not earned by moral performance but granted by union. Sproul: “The love that casts out fear (v. 18) is grounded not in our lovableness but in Christ's righteousness, in which we stand.”
